about: A letter saying a household was paid too much SNAP (a claim): the hearing date, repayment and what the state can take.

rows.plain: A SNAP claim is one of three kinds: an intentional program violation, a household mistake, or an agency mistake. The letter must say which kind it is and why.
Unless a hearing already set the amount, the household has 90 days to ask for a fair hearing about the claim.
The date to pay or make an arrangement is set by the letter and is no later than 30 days after the first notice.
The letter must give the amount, the months covered, how it was worked out and a phone number, and must say you can look at the records.
You can make a written agreement to repay in installments before the claim is sent for federal collection.
For a household mistake or an agency mistake, the state can take the greater of $10 a month or 10% of the monthly SNAP amount, unless the household agrees to more.
For an intentional program violation, the state can take the greater of $20 a month or 20% of the monthly SNAP amount.
A state may lower (compromise) a claim when the household's finances show it will not be paid in three years.
A claim is delinquent when it is not paid by its due date and there is no payment arrangement, or when an installment is missed.
A claim that has been delinquent for 180 days or more must be sent to the Treasury Offset Program, which can take federal payments such as tax refunds.
A claim is worked out back to at least 12 months before the state learned of the overpayment, and never for months more than six years before that.
Before a hearing you can look at the documents the state will use and get a free copy of the relevant parts of your case file. Someone else, such as a lawyer or a friend, can present your case.
The state has 60 days from getting a hearing request to hold the hearing, decide and tell the household.
